name: market-swipe-all-pay-first
about: Every saved competitor ad leads with pay on a truck on the road, beside BLS pay. The plan may use that to choose an angle that differs from what the market shows — and must write no figure from those ads.

area.label: Fixture Yard, IL
area.reason: Fixture: drivers within a day's drive of the yard.

subject_matter.in_our_words: A small fleet where dispatch knows your name

history.text: Boostpoint 2026 benchmark, CDL drivers on Meta: an ad costing more than $42.00 per lead after 5 leads, or $85.00 spent with no lead, is where pausing is suggested.

BLS wage survey, 2025: heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers in Illinois, the state this ad's area is centred in, earned a median of $60,320 a year ($29.00 an hour); a tenth earned $39,710 or less and a tenth $86,300 or more.
BLS wage survey, 2025: heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers across the United States earned a median of $58,640 a year ($28.19 an hour); a tenth earned $40,140 or less and a tenth $79,380 or more.

A competitor's ad saved by our recruiters ("seen on Facebook"). What it leads with: pay first. What its picture shows: truck on the road. It offers OTR work paid by the mile. Its words, as read: "$0.65 PER MILE, / CLASS A OTR. / APPLY TODAY".

A competitor's ad saved by our recruiters. What it leads with: pay first. What its picture shows: truck on the road. It offers regional work with weekly pay. Its words, as read: "$1,800 a week / Home weekends".

output.audience: Class A drivers who meet the experience requirement, pull or want to pull flatbed, and live near Midwest lanes. Many run OTR or sit in large fleets, out longer than a week at a time. A stated pay per mile, home weekly and an assigned truck at a small fleet would make them stop.

angles.idea: Lead with the pay per mile for regional flatbed work, with home weekly right beside it.
angles.proof: The job states the pay per mile and that the driver is home weekly.
angles.why: Competitors' saved ads lead with pay over a truck on the road, so drivers compare rates there. Ours holds up beside the OTR ad's rate. Nothing has been measured for this carrier yet.

angles.idea: Lead with getting home weekly from Midwest regional lanes, pictured as the street a driver comes back to.
angles.proof: The job states home weekly and that the lanes are in the Midwest.
angles.why: A competitor's regional ad sells home time with a truck on the road; a home street shows the result instead. Nothing has been measured for this carrier, so this is a test.

angles.idea: Lead with the assigned truck and the flatbed it pulls, parked and ready for its driver.
angles.proof: The job states an assigned truck and flatbed work.
angles.why: An assigned truck is a fact the saved competitor ads do not mention, and naming flatbed draws drivers who do that work. Nothing has been measured for this carrier yet.

angles.idea: Say plainly who the job is for: Class A, the stated experience, flatbed, Midwest lanes.
angles.proof: The job states the licence class, the experience requirement, flatbed and Midwest lanes.
angles.why: No lead outcomes exist yet, so stating the requirement and the area up front is the cheapest way to keep out drivers who cannot take the job. Nothing has been measured.

angles.idea: Set the offer out as a plain list of stated terms, ending on a small fleet where dispatch knows your name.
angles.proof: The job states the pay per mile, home weekly, the retirement plan and the carrier's own line about dispatch.
angles.why: The competitors' ads give a pay line and little else; the full terms on a plain ground let a driver check the offer. Nothing has been measured, so treat this as a test.
